elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New § 11.3: "Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". Corio is the customer under this Agreement (Commerce One is the licensor/host); the element is disjunctive and there is no Order Form structure in this document, so the Agreement-level right suffices. Naming Corio rather than "Customer" is correct because § 1.6 defines "CUSTOMER(S)" as Corio's sublicensees. The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a literal alias-matching artifact and does not reflect substance.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: § 11.3 requires "thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly the 30-day ceiling, in writing.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: § 11.3: "Commerce One shall refund to Corio, pro rata, any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination." The refund is expressly pro rata (not merely post-termination-period), runs from Vendor to Customer, and is triggered by the convenience termination.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: § 11.3 second sentence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." Retained § 11.1 lets either party give notice "at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration" of the then-current term — that is natural-term non-renewal effective at expiry (a RENEWAL matter), not a mid-term Vendor convenience exit, so no contradiction arises. Retained § 11.2 exits are for-cause (breach/insolvency).

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: § 11.3 sets 30 days' notice, which is outside the 60–90 day fallback band. This is more favourable to us but literally fails the fallback element; irrelevant because the preferred level is complete.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the redline imposes no early-termination fee, and no retained provision (§§ 11.1–11.2) contains a termination penalty, so no fee can exceed a three-month cap.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply in a stronger form: § 11.3 removes any Vendor convenience right during the initial or any renewal term, so Vendor has no convenience termination at all; § 11.1's non-renewal notice is expressly tied to expiration of the then-current term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Vendor holds no convenience termination right under § 11.3, so no notice period for such a right is required.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: the single inserted § 11.3 delivers all four preferred elements (Customer convenience right, 30 days' written notice, pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, express bar on Vendor convenience termination during the initial and renewal terms).

The 'deviation' classification is correct on the original text: § 11.1 commits to a five-year initial term and § 11.2 permits exit only for uncured material breach or insolvency, so no Customer convenience right exists in a multi-year term — a failure of both preferred and fallback.

Minimal: the redline is a concise insertion into the existing Section 11 numbering scheme; §§ 11.1 and 11.2 are retained verbatim, no favourable language is deleted, and the drafter correctly omitted the model language's surplus 'in whole or in part' because there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure. No survival tail, expense allocation, procedure, or other extra-checklist requirement was added.

Preserves intent: the for-cause and insolvency exits, the term/auto-renewal mechanic, and the § 11.1 mutual non-renewal notice survive without contradiction; no undefined term or dangling cross-reference is created. Using 'Corio' rather than 'Customer' avoids a definitional conflict with § 1.6 ('CUSTOMER(S)' = Corio's sublicensees).

Note for the drafter: the deterministic signal 'Customer convenience termination present = false' is an alias-matching artifact (the clause names Corio, the customer party, not the literal token 'Customer') and does not indicate a substantive gap; no repair is needed.

Fallback is not independently satisfied only because the notice period is 30 days rather than 60–90 days; that is a Customer-favourable deviation and does not affect completeness at the preferred level. The margin comment's offer of the 60–90 day/three-month-fee fallback is properly framed as a concession, not as operative text.
